title: Capstone — Build Your Personal AI Knowledge Engine

sections.content:
## What You're Building

This capstone produces a complete, personal AI knowledge system — something you'll actually use every day after this course ends. By the time you finish, you'll have:

1. **A curated prompt library** — 20+ prompts tuned to your specific work, organised by task type
2. **A NotebookLM research corpus** — a searchable knowledge base on your most important professional topic
3. **A Claude Project** — a custom AI assistant that knows your context, preferences, and domain
4. **A personal AI workflow document** — documenting exactly how you use AI daily, so you can replicate and improve it
5. **An agent delegation brief template** — ready to use for your most automation-worthy task

This is not a demo. Everything you build today is production-ready and starts delivering value immediately.

**Time estimate:** The full capstone is 90 minutes. If you're short on time, Phase 1 + Phase 2 (prompt library + Claude Project) can be done in 40 minutes and deliver the most immediate value. Complete the rest in a follow-up session — your work saves automatically.

## Phase 1: Build Your Prompt Library (20 minutes)

A prompt library is a collection of your best, tested prompts — tuned for your specific context, role, and tools. It means you never start from a blank prompt again.

**Step 1 — Identify your top 10 AI use cases (5 minutes)**

Open a blank document and list the 10 types of tasks you do with AI most often. Be specific:

| Your generic task | Specific version |
|---|---|
| "Write emails" | "Draft client follow-up after a proposal meeting" |
| "Summarise documents" | "Summarise a 30-page audit report for my manager" |
| "Research" | "Find competitor pricing for enterprise SaaS tools" |
| "Plan" | "Create a project plan for a 3-month website redesign" |

Write your 10 specific tasks.

**Step 2 — Generate tuned prompts for each (10 minutes)**

For each task, use this meta-prompt in Claude to generate an optimised prompt:
```
I need an optimised prompt for the following task:

Task: [your specific task]
My role/context: [your job title, company type, industry]
Audience for the output: [who reads/uses the result]
Format I prefer: [bullet points / paragraphs / tables / etc.]
Tone: [formal / professional / conversational]
Length: [short / medium / detailed]
Special requirements: [anything task-specific — e.g., "always include a call to action", "cite sources", "use Australian English"]

Write the best possible prompt for this task. Include [PLACEHOLDERS] for the parts I'll fill in each time. After the prompt, briefly explain what you included and why.
```

**Step 3 — Test and refine (5 minutes)**

For your 3 most important tasks, run the generated prompt with real content. Rate the output 1-10. For any below 7, ask:
```
This prompt produced an output I'd rate 6/10. Here's what I got: [paste output]
Here's what I wanted instead: [describe the gap]
Refine the prompt to produce what I'm looking for.
```

**Step 4 — Organise your library**

Create a document called `prompt-library.md` (or a Notion page) with this structure:
```
# My AI Prompt Library
Last updated: [date]

## Writing
### [Task name]
**When to use:** [one sentence]
**Prompt:**
[full prompt with placeholders]
**Notes:** [any tips on filling it in]

## Research
[same structure]

## Planning
[same structure]

## Analysis
[same structure]
```

This library compounds over time. Every prompt you refine and save is one you never have to write again.

## Phase 2: Set Up Your Claude Project (15 minutes)

A Claude Project is a persistent AI assistant that knows your context, has access to your documents, and maintains consistent instructions across every conversation. This is the single highest-leverage Claude feature for professional users.

**Step 1 — Create your main work project**

In Claude.ai → Projects → New Project.

Name it for your primary work context: "[Your Role] — [Company/Domain]"
Examples: "Product Manager — Fintech", "Research Analyst — Healthcare", "Freelance Designer"

**Step 2 — Write your Project Instruction (10 minutes)**

This is the most important thing you'll write in this capstone. Take your time with it. Use this template:

```
## Context
I am [your name], [your role] at [company type/description]. My work focuses on [primary domain]. My team/clients are [description].

## What this project is for
This project contains [list what documents you'll upload]. Use it to help me with [primary use cases].

## How I work
- Communication style: I prefer [formal/direct/concise/detailed]
- Format preference: [bullet points for lists / headers for long content / tables for comparisons]
- Length preference: [default to concise; I'll ask if I want more]
- Australian/British/American English: [specify]

## Always
- Cite specific documents when referencing project materials
- Flag if you're uncertain or if information might be outdated
- If I give you a rough draft, improve the substance not just the words
- When I ask for analysis, give me your actual opinion, not just a list of options

## Never
- Pad responses with filler phrases ("Certainly!", "Great question!", etc.)
- Include disclaimers I didn't ask for
- Recommend things outside my context (if I ask for a marketing strategy, don't suggest hiring an agency)

## Domain context
[2-3 paragraphs of important context about your domain, company, industry, or work that would help Claude give better answers. This is your chance to share background that would take many conversations to establish otherwise.]

## Key terminology
[Any specialised terms in your domain that Claude might not interpret correctly — your company's names for things, industry-specific abbreviations, etc.]
```

**Step 3 — Upload your core documents**

Upload 3-7 documents that represent your core working knowledge:
- Company overview or product documentation (non-confidential)
- Key reference documents for your domain
- Style guides or brand guidelines
- Previously written examples of your best work
- Frameworks or templates you use regularly

After uploading, test with:
```
Based on the documents in this project, give me a brief overview of what you know about [your domain]. What are the most important things I should know that you now have access to?
```

If Claude doesn't reference the documents accurately, re-read the upload to ensure they loaded correctly.

## Phase 3: Build Your Research Knowledge Base in NotebookLM (20 minutes)

Choose your single most important professional topic — the area where you most need to stay informed, where you have the most documents, or where you most often search for information.

**Step 1 — Gather 6-10 sources (10 minutes)**

For your chosen topic, collect:
- 2-3 foundational reference documents (PDFs — reports, guides, standards)
- 2-3 recent research or industry reports (find on Google Scholar, industry associations, or company blogs)
- 1-2 framework documents (methodologies, best practices, frameworks you work with)
- 1 document of your own notes or previous work on this topic

**Quality tip:** Better to have 6 excellent, highly relevant documents than 15 loosely related ones. RAG precision decreases with noise.

**Step 2 — Create and populate the notebook (5 minutes)**

1. New notebook at notebooklm.google.com
2. Name it precisely: "[Topic] — Reference Corpus — [Year]"
3. Upload all sources
4. Wait for indexing

**Step 3 — Run your First Queries (5 minutes)**

Test your knowledge base with real questions you'd normally have to manually search for:
```
What are the most important principles or frameworks across these documents?
```
```
[Specific question you'd normally Google] — based on these documents
```
```
What do these documents NOT cover that someone working in this area would also need to know?
```
```
Create a structured FAQ of the 10 most important questions in this domain, with answers from these sources
```

**Step 4 — Generate the Audio Overview**

Click "Generate" → "Audio Overview." Download it. This 10-15 minute AI podcast is a condensed briefing on everything in your knowledge base — listen to it while commuting or exercising. It updates your mental model faster than re-reading the documents.

## Phase 4: Design Your Daily AI Workflow (15 minutes)

The most effective AI users have an intentional daily workflow — they don't open an AI tool and hope inspiration strikes. They know which task goes where and in what order.

**Step 1 — Map your typical workday AI touchpoints**

For each time of day, list what you do and which AI tool helps:

```
MORNING ROUTINE (first 30 minutes)
- Check email: [tool] for [what — draft replies, prioritise, summarise threads]
- Review calendar: [tool] for [what — prepare for meetings, research participants]
- Read industry news: [tool] for [what — summarise, flag relevant items]

DEEP WORK
- [Your primary task type]: [tool] for [what specifically]
- [Second primary task]: [tool] for [what specifically]

MEETINGS
- Before: [tool] for preparation
- During: [tool if any — Otter.ai, Teams Copilot, etc.]
- After: [tool] for notes and action items

END OF DAY
- Status update: [tool] for drafting
- Planning tomorrow: [tool] for prioritisation
```

**Step 2 — Identify your one highest-leverage AI habit**

Look at your map. Which single change would save you the most time or produce the most value *every day*?

Commit to making it a consistent habit for 2 weeks.

**Step 3 — Write your workflow document**

Ask Claude to help you formalise it:
```
Here are my AI touchpoints throughout the day: [paste your map]

Help me write a "My AI Workflow" document that:
1. Describes my workflow clearly enough that I could share it with a new team member
2. Lists the specific tools and prompts for each task type
3. Notes the tasks where I'm NOT using AI but probably should be
4. Includes a "how to get started" section for the three most impactful items
```

Save this document. Review it in 30 days and update based on what's actually working.

## Phase 5: Create Your Agent Delegation Brief Template (10 minutes)

The final piece: a reusable template for delegating tasks to AI agents. Once you have this template, any repetitive multi-step task can be converted into an agent brief in 5 minutes.

**The Agent Delegation Brief template:**

```markdown
# Agent Delegation Brief

## Task
[Clear, specific description of what the agent should accomplish]

## Goal / Success Criteria
[What does 'done' look like? How will I know it succeeded?]

## Scope
IN scope:
- [List what IS included]

OUT of scope:
- [List what is explicitly excluded]

## Resources Available
The agent has access to:
- [Tool 1: web search / files / email / calendar / etc.]
- [Tool 2]
- [Any specific documents or data]

## Constraints
- Do NOT: [actions it must not take without checking first]
- If uncertain about X: [how to handle ambiguity]
- If you encounter Y: [specific fallback behaviour]

## Output Format
[Exactly how the output should be structured]

## Before Completing
Verify:
- [ ] [Quality check 1]
- [ ] [Quality check 2]
- [ ] No action taken that cannot be reversed

## Report Back
Include in your completion report:
- What you did and in what order
- What you found
- Anything you couldn't complete and why
- Recommended next steps
```

**Fill this in for your first agent task:**

Choose the one task from your daily workflow that is:
- Repetitive (you do it regularly)
- Multi-step (more than 3 steps)
- Well-defined (clear success criteria)
- Currently time-consuming

Write a delegation brief for it using the template above. You now have a reusable document for delegating this task to Claude Code, Claude Research, or any other agentic tool.

sections.title: The Full Build — 90-Minute Knowledge Engine
sections.content:
This is your build session. Execute all 5 phases. Check off each item as you complete it.

**PHASE 1 — Prompt Library** (target: 20 minutes)
- [ ] Listed 10 specific AI use cases for my work
- [ ] Used meta-prompting to generate tuned prompts for all 10
- [ ] Tested and refined the 3 most important prompts
- [ ] Created `prompt-library.md` with all prompts organised by category
- [ ] Added at least one prompt with the XML structure from lesson 18-1

**PHASE 2 — Claude Project** (target: 15 minutes)
- [ ] Created a new Claude Project named for my primary work context
- [ ] Wrote a comprehensive Project Instruction using the template
- [ ] Uploaded 3-7 relevant documents
- [ ] Tested that Claude accurately references the uploaded documents
- [ ] Claude can answer at least 3 real work questions using the project context

**PHASE 3 — NotebookLM Corpus** (target: 20 minutes)
- [ ] Chose my single most important professional topic
- [ ] Collected 6-10 high-quality sources
- [ ] Created and populated a NotebookLM notebook
- [ ] Ran 5 real queries and verified citation accuracy
- [ ] Generated the Audio Overview (downloaded for offline listening)

**PHASE 4 — Daily Workflow** (target: 15 minutes)
- [ ] Mapped AI touchpoints throughout my workday
- [ ] Identified the one highest-leverage habit to commit to
- [ ] Created a "My AI Workflow" document with Claude's help
- [ ] Scheduled a 30-day review in my calendar

**PHASE 5 — Agent Brief** (target: 10 minutes)
- [ ] Identified my best candidate task for agent delegation
- [ ] Filled in the Agent Delegation Brief template for that task
- [ ] Saved the template somewhere I'll find it

---

**After completing all phases, answer these reflection questions:**

1. **What changed?** Compare how you'll work with AI next week vs. how you worked before this course. What's the single biggest difference?

2. **What surprised you?** Was there a technique, tool, or approach that worked better than you expected?

3. **What's your next learning priority?** After 18 parts, what AI capability do you most want to develop further?

4. **Who would benefit from this?** Which colleague, friend, or team would get the most value from learning what you learned in this course? Consider sharing your prompt library with them as a starting point.

---

**Your deliverables from this capstone:**
- `prompt-library.md` — 10+ tuned prompts for your work
- Claude Project — a persistent AI assistant that knows your context
- NotebookLM notebook — a queryable knowledge base on your professional topic
- `my-ai-workflow.md` — your documented daily AI workflow
- `agent-brief-template.md` — reusable delegation template

These five artifacts are your personal AI operating system. They compound over time: every prompt you refine makes the library better, every document you add makes the knowledge base richer, every agent brief you write makes delegation faster.

The goal was never to teach you about AI. The goal was to make AI something you actually use, every day, better than almost anyone you know.

sections.title: Workshop A — Knowledge Engine Architecture
sections.content:
Design your personal knowledge engine before building it.

**Step 1 — Inventory your knowledge sources:**
- How many documents/notes do you have? (rough count)
- What formats? (markdown, PDF, web pages, emails)
- How are they currently organised? (folder structure, tags)
- How do you currently search them?

**Step 2 — Define your use case precisely:** What questions do you want your knowledge engine to answer? "Search my notes" is too vague. "Answer questions about technical decisions I've made in the last year" is specific.

**Step 3 — Ask Claude to design the architecture:**
"Design a personal knowledge engine for [your use case]. What indexing strategy, chunking approach, and query interface would best serve this specific use case?"

**Step 4 — Validate feasibility:** Can you build this in [your time budget] with your current skills? What's the MVP version?

sections.title: Workshop B — Build and Index
sections.content:
Build and populate your personal knowledge engine.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude Code** to implement the ingestion pipeline based on your architecture design.

**Step 2 — Start with a subset** of your documents (50-100) for initial testing.

**Step 3 — Run the ingestion.** Does it complete without errors? How long does it take?

**Step 4 — Query the engine** with 10 test questions that your documents should be able to answer.

**Step 5 — Measure retrieval quality:** For each question, rate 1-5 whether the retrieved chunks were relevant.

**Step 6 — Improve the configuration** (chunk size, overlap, number of results retrieved) based on the quality assessment.

sections.title: Workshop C — Query Interface Design
sections.content:
Design a query interface that makes your knowledge engine actually usable.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude:** "What makes a knowledge engine interface actually useful vs technically correct but frustrating to use? What interface elements are most important?"

**Step 2 — Design your interface:**
- Query input (how do you enter questions?)
- Result display (how are answers shown?)
- Source display (which documents were used?)
- Confidence indicator (how certain is the answer?)
- Navigation (can you open the source documents?)

**Step 3 — Ask Claude Code** to implement the interface based on your design.

**Step 4 — Use the engine for one week** for real work. What friction points emerge?

sections.title: Workshop D — Expand and Maintain
sections.content:
Scale your knowledge engine and establish maintenance routines.

**Step 1 — Expand the index** to include all your relevant documents.

**Step 2 — Set up automatic updates:** When new documents are added to your knowledge sources, they should automatically be indexed.

**Step 3 — Establish a maintenance routine:**
- Monthly: check that the index is current
- Quarterly: review query logs for common questions that produce poor results
- Annually: evaluate whether the architecture still fits your needs

**Step 4 — Measure actual usage impact:** After one month, has the knowledge engine changed how you work? What would you do differently?

sections.question: Your knowledge engine returns an answer that confidently cites a specific document, but when you check the document, the cited information isn't there. What is happening?
options: The document was deleted from the index
Hallucination: the LLM may have generated a plausible-sounding citation that doesn't match actual retrieved content. Always display the exact retrieved chunks alongside the answer
The retrieval system has a bug
The document format wasn't parsed correctly
sections.explanation: RAG systems can still hallucinate citations and content even when documents are retrieved. The LLM might: reference a document by name but make up the specific detail, generate a plausible quote that isn't in the source, or misattribute content from one document to another. Mitigation: always display the actual retrieved text chunks alongside the answer so users can verify. Ideally, the interface shows: "Based on this passage from [document]: [exact quote]" rather than just an answer.

sections.question: Your knowledge engine works well on recent documents but poorly on documents from 3 years ago. What is the most likely cause?
options: Older documents use outdated language that models can't understand
Old documents may use different terminology or writing styles — the embedding model creates different representations for older vocabulary, reducing semantic match with modern query language
The embedding model was trained after those documents were written
Older documents are too long to be indexed correctly
sections.explanation: Vocabulary drift affects retrieval quality. Concepts described with older terminology may not match the embedding space for modern query language, even if the concepts are the same. For example, "machine learning" queries might not retrieve documents about "artificial intelligence" from the early 2010s. Mitigation: (1) query expansion — have the LLM generate older synonyms before retrieval, (2) add a date-aware search layer, (3) tag old documents with modern synonym annotations during ingestion.

sections.content:
**You've completed the AI Mastery Course.**

You've covered 18 parts — from what AI is, to how LLMs work, through prompting, tools, Claude Code, MCP servers, local models, automation, agents, research workflows, office tools, project management, and now advanced mastery. You've built real things, established real habits, and grounded everything in actual use rather than theory.

The field will keep moving. Models will improve. New tools will appear. But the framework you have now — how to evaluate tools critically, how to prompt effectively, how to build knowledge systems, how to delegate to agents — that framework holds. The learner who finishes this course isn't behind the technology. They're positioned to adopt every new capability that comes, faster than anyone starting fresh.

Use it well.
